mainTopic: Taking back a former חבר or גבאי, when a person may judge his own animals and food, and how blemished sacred animals are sold
overview: This amud brings several ברייתות and then starts a new chapter. The first ברייתא asks whether someone who took on the strict practices of a חבר and then dropped them can be accepted again. רבי מאיר says never. רבי יהודה says it depends on private versus public conduct, and the גמרא gives two versions of his view. רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה say he is always accepted, and רבי יוחנן rules like them. A second ברייתא says that a חבר who became a גבאי was at first never taken back, but later the חכמים ruled that once he quits he is like anyone else. A story about רב הונא בר חייא shows רב יוסף and רבה each citing a different clause of that ברייתא. A third ברייתא teaches that a יחיד מומחה may not inspect his own בכור, but he may inspect his own קדשים and מעשר and rule on his own טהרות, because in those cases he has no real motive to lie. The chapter עד כמה ישראל חייבין then ends. A new משנה teaches that פסולי המוקדשין are sold and weighed in the market because their profit goes to הקדש, while בכור and מעשר are not, because their profit goes to the owner.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: Those who backslide are never accepted again
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records רבי מאיר's view that anyone who accepted the status of a חבר and then gave it up can never be accepted again.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: All of those who went back on their commitment are never accepted again. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא about people who took on the strict practices of a חבר and later dropped them. רבי מאיר says they can never get that trusted status back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'כולן' refers to the people discussed just before this, who had accepted the practices of a חבר. Once such a person has shown he can break his commitment, רבי מאיר holds that he has lost our trust forever. A second קבלה does not help.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages taught (introduces a ברייתא)
They went back on their commitment
We do not accept them (back as a חבר)
Ever, permanently

steps.confusionAlert: 'Not accepted' does not mean he is thrown out of the Jewish people or cannot do תשובה before ה׳. It only means he is not trusted again with the special status of a חבר.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
And all of them who retracted (went back to being עמי הארץ)
are never accepted again,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the ברייתא and gives the first, strictest opinion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי מאיר, a חבר who backslid is never accepted again.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: Hidden backsliding versus open backsliding
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה makes a distinction. If he backslid secretly, he is not accepted. If he backslid openly, he is accepted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: If they went back in secret, they are not accepted. If they went back in public, they are accepted.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a second, middle opinion. For רבי יהודה, the answer depends on how the person abandoned his practices.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person who drops his practices in secret, while still acting like a חבר in public, is showing that he is two-faced. We cannot trust him. A person who backslides openly is at least honest about where he stands, so if he wants to return, we can believe him.

keyTerms.meaning: In secret, in hidden places
In public, openly

steps.confusionAlert: It seems backwards, since public sinning sounds worse. But the issue here is honesty. The secret backslider is the one who fooled people, so he is the one we cannot trust.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
If they went back (to their old ways) in secret,
they are not accepted;
if in public, they are accepted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי מאיר by giving a middle position.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who backslid secretly is not accepted. Someone who backslid openly is accepted.

steps.title: A second version of רבי יהודה's distinction
steps.stepSummary: Some report רבי יהודה's view differently. It depends on whether his original practice as a חבר was kept even in private, or only in public.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are those who say: If they did their practices even in private, they are accepted. If only in public, they are not accepted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings an alternate version (איכא דאמרי) of how to read רבי יהודה's opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, the question is not how he backslid. It is how sincere he was when he first acted as a חבר. If he kept the practices even when no one was watching, he was sincere, so we take him back. If he kept them only for show, his return is not trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say (an alternate version)
They performed their practices

steps.confusionAlert: Notice that the result is flipped compared to the first version. Here, 'private' leads to being accepted and 'public' leads to not being accepted, because the words now refer to his earlier good conduct, not to his backsliding.

phrases.english: There are those who say:
If they performed their practices (as a חבר) even in private,
they are accepted;
if only in public, they are not accepted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different version of the distinction in Step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, if he kept the practices even privately, he is accepted. If he kept them only publicly, he is not.

steps.title: רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה: Always accepted
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה say the person is accepted in every case, based on the פסוק 'Return, backsliding children.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה say: Either way they are accepted, as it says, 'Return, you backsliding children.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings the most lenient opinion, backed by a פסוק from ירמיהו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ה׳ Himself calls on those who strayed to come back. So we should also welcome a person who wants to return to being a חבר. 'Either way' means it does not matter whether the case was private or public.

keyTerms.meaning: Either way, in both cases
Return, backsliding children (ירמיהו ג:כב)

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה אוֹמְרִים:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha say:

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין כָּךְ וּבֵין כָּךְ מְקַבְּלִין אוֹתָן,
phrases.english: Either way, they are accepted,
because it is stated:
"Return, you backsliding children."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה אוֹמְרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects both רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה with a fully lenient view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A returning backslider is always accepted again, based on the פסוק.

steps.title: The halacha follows the lenient pair
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that the הלכה follows רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק איש כפר עכו said in the name of רבי יוחנן: The הלכה follows that pair.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the disagreement in favor of the lenient opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'That pair' means the two תנאים in Step 4. So in practice, anyone who left the status of a חבר and wants to return is accepted, no matter how he left.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical law follows...
Pair (of Sages)

steps.whatToRemember: There are three views: never accepted (רבי מאיר), it depends on private versus public (רבי יהודה, in two versions), and always accepted (רבי שמעון and רבי יהושע בן קרחה). The הלכה is that he is always accepted.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק אִישׁ כְּפַר עַכּוֹ
phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak of the village of Akko said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
The halacha is in accordance with that pair.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the מחלוקת in favor of Step 4.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A backslider who wants to return to being a חבר is accepted in all cases.

steps.title: Original rule: A חבר who becomes a tax collector loses his status for good
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא says that at first, a חבר who became a גבאי was removed from his status, and even after quitting he was not taken back.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: Originally they would say that a חבר who became a tax collector is pushed out of his status as a חבר. If he quit, he is still not accepted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא on a related case: a חבר who takes the job of collecting taxes. This step gives the earlier ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tax collectors were suspected of dishonesty, so taking the job cost him his trusted status. Under the original ruling, even quitting the job did not undo the damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Originally, at first
Tax collector
They push away, remove
Status as a חבר
He quit, separated himself (from the job)

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
Originally they would say:
A חבר who became a tax collector,
they remove him from his status as a חבר;
if he quit, he is (still) not accepted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ברייתא on a related topic: losing the status of a חבר because of a job.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Originally, a חבר who became a tax collector lost his status permanently, even after quitting.

steps.title: Later rule: Once he quits, he is like anyone else
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים later changed the rule. A tax collector who quits is treated like any ordinary person and can become a חבר again.
steps.simpleTranslation: They went back and said: If he quit, he is like any other person.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends by giving the later, more lenient ruling, which replaces the original one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once he leaves the suspicious job, there is no longer any reason to distrust him. He stands like any other person who wants to accept the practices of a חבר. This matches the welcoming attitude of the הלכה in Step 5.

keyTerms.meaning: They changed their ruling, they went back and said
Like any person

steps.whatToRemember: The later ruling is the one that stands. A חבר who became a tax collector and then quit can be accepted again like anyone else.

phrases.english: They went back to saying:
If he quit, he is like any other person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Overturns the original rule in Step 6.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A former tax collector who quits is treated like anyone else and may become a חבר again.

steps.title: The story of רב הונא בר חייא becoming a tax collector
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים honored רב הונא בר חייא. When he became a גבאי they cut him off, and when he quit, רבה went back to him but רב יוסף did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: One time the חכמים needed רב הונא בר חייא. רבה, רב יוסף, and four hundred pairs of חכמים came to him. When he heard they were coming, he set up four hundred chairs for them. Later they heard he had become a tax collector. They sent him a message: 'Go to your important new job, go back to your old status.' He sent back: 'I have repented.' רב יוסף did not go to him, but רבה did.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real-life story that shows the rule about a tax collector who quits. The two great חכמים acted differently, and the next step explains why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first רב הונא בר חייא was highly respected. Becoming a גבאי cost him that respect, so the חכמים cut him off. Once he quit, רבה and רב יוסף split on whether to accept him back, which matches the two stages of the ברייתא in Steps 6 and 7.

keyTerms.meaning: A tax collector, who was suspected of dishonesty
Chairs or seats
'Go to your importance.' A sharp way of saying 'enjoy your new job, we don't need you'
'I have taken it back.' He repented and quit the job

phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Chiyya
one time he was needed (the Sages needed him),

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה עָיֵיל גַּבֵּיהּ רַבָּה וְרַב יוֹסֵף
phrases.english: Rabba and Rav Yosef went in to him
and four hundred pairs of Sages.
He heard that they were coming,
and he tied together four hundred chairs for them.
Eventually they heard that he had become a tax collector.
They sent him a message:
Go to your importance, go back to your former status.
He sent to them: I have repented.

phrases.aramaic: רַב יוֹסֵף לָא אֲזַל, רַבָּה אֲזַל.
phrases.english: Rav Yosef did not go to him; Rabba went.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא בַּר חִיָּיא אִיצְטְרִיכָא לֵיהּ שַׁעְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A real-life story that applies the two-stage rule from Steps 6 and 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In practice, the חכמים split on whether to accept back a former גבאי who repented.

steps.title: רב יוסף and רבה each explain what they did
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף relies on the early rule that a former גבאי is not accepted. רבה relies on the later rule that he is like anyone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: We learned that if he quits, we do not accept him. רבה said: We learned that the חכמים later went back and said that if he quits, he is like any other person.
steps.whatsHappening: Each חכם explains his behavior by quoting the ברייתא about a former גבאי as he learned it. The גמרא does not say why רב יוסף quoted only the earlier rule. One possibility is that his version of the ברייתא lacked the later change.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף quotes only the line that someone who quit is not accepted. רבה quotes the continuation of the ברייתא, 'חזרו לומר': the חכמים later ruled that once he quits, he is like an ordinary person. The גמרא does not explain why רב יוסף relied on the earlier line. Perhaps his version lacked the change, or perhaps he had another reason.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We have learned it.' Introduces a source from a ברייתא or משנה
He quit (left the tax-collecting job)
'They went back and said.' The חכמים changed their earlier ruling
Like any ordinary person

steps.whatToRemember: A גבאי who truly quits is treated like anyone else and may become a חבר again. This is the later rule, and רבה acted on it.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא does not explain why רב יוסף relied on the earlier line ('פירש אין מקבלין אותו') when the ברייתא records a later change ('חזרו לומר'). One possible explanation is that his version lacked the change, but the text itself does not say so.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: We learned:
if he quit, we do not accept him.
Rabba said: We learned:
they went back and said:
if he quit, he is like any other person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the different behavior in the story of Step 8.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבה acted on the later ruling (Step 7), so a repentant former גבאי can be accepted back.

steps.title: A new ברייתא: who may inspect a בכור for a blemish
steps.stepSummary: A person may inspect any בכור except his own. He may still inspect his own קדשים and מעשר, and decide about the purity of his own food.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: A person may inspect all firstborn animals for blemishes, except his own. He may inspect his own consecrated animals and his own tithe animals, and he may decide questions about the purity of his own food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It brings a ברייתא about when a person may judge his own animals or food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Today a בכור may only be eaten if it has a blemish, so its owner benefits if it is declared blemished. That is why he may not inspect his own בכור. Even so, the ברייתא lets him inspect his own קדשים and מעשר, and trusts him about his own טהרות.

keyTerms.meaning: Firstborn kosher animals, which are holy and given to a כהן
Inspects the animal to judge whether it has a blemish
His animals that were consecrated to the בית המקדש
His tithe animals (מעשר בהמה)
His foods that must stay ritually pure

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A person may inspect all firstborns,
except for his own,
and he may inspect his own consecrated animals,
and his own tithe animals,
and he may rule on questions about his own pure foods.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: כׇּל הַבְּכוֹרוֹת אָדָם רוֹאֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: trusting a person who has a personal interest.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person may not inspect his own בכור, but he may inspect his own קדשים and מעשר, and may rule on his own טהרות.

steps.title: What case is the ברייתא talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the first line of the ברייתא and asks what situation it means.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: A person may inspect all firstborns except his own. What case are we dealing with?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא and asks what case it describes. This sets up the next two steps, which test each possible answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is how many people are inspecting the animal. Is it one person alone, or a group of three? Each option will cause a problem.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Master said.' Quotes a line from the source being discussed
'What case are we dealing with?'

phrases.english: The Master said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הַבְּכוֹרוֹת אָדָם רוֹאֶה חוּץ מִשֶּׁל עַצְמוֹ.
phrases.english: A person may inspect all firstborns except for his own.
What case are we dealing with?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: כׇּל הַבְּכוֹרוֹת אָדָם רוֹאֶה חוּץ מִשֶּׁל עַצְמוֹ. בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts analyzing the ברייתא from Step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the ברייתא talking about one inspector alone, or a panel of three?

steps.title: It cannot mean one person alone
steps.stepSummary: If it means one ordinary person, he is not trusted on anyone's בכור, so why mention 'except his own'?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it means one person, is he trusted at all?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the first possible answer, one inspector, and rejects it right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה later (36b) says an ordinary person cannot permit a בכור alone; it takes three. So one person cannot permit even someone else's בכור. Saying 'except his own' would add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: 'If you say.' Introduces a possible answer that will be tested
'Is he trusted?' Here it means: of course he is not

steps.confusionAlert: 'מי מהימן' sounds like a real question, but it is rhetorical. It means 'he is not trusted at all.'

phrases.english: If you say it means one person,
is he trusted?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the first possible answer to Step 11 and rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects reading the ברייתא as one person inspecting alone.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: One ordinary person cannot permit any בכור, so 'except his own' would be pointless.

steps.title: It cannot mean three either: a judge is not suspected
steps.stepSummary: If it means a panel of three, the owner should not be suspected. A judge may marry a woman who did מיאון or חליצה before him, because he was only part of a בית דין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it must mean three people. But are they suspected? Didn't we learn in a משנה: if a woman did מיאון or חליצה in front of a judge, he may marry her, because he acted as part of a court!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the second possible answer, three inspectors, and challenges it with a משנה from יבמות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With three judges, no single member decides alone. So the owner being one of the three should not be a problem. The proof is the משנה in יבמות 25b. A judge may marry a woman whose מיאון or חליצה took place before him. We do not suspect him of bending the ruling, because he was only one member of a בית דין.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Are they suspected?' A rhetorical way of saying they should not be
'But we learned in a משנה!' Introduces a source that challenges the idea
She did מיאון: a girl married as a minor refuses the marriage
She did חליצה, the ceremony that frees a widow from יבום
A court of three judges

steps.whyThisMatters: Both options seem to fail. This forces the גמרא to find a new explanation of the ברייתא, which it gives in Step 14.

phrases.english: Rather, it means three people.
But are they suspected?
Didn't we learn in a mishna:
if she did refusal or chalitza in front of him,
he may marry her,
because he acted as part of a court!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting 'one person,' the גמרא tries 'three people' and challenges that too.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading the ברייתא as a panel of three that includes the owner.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A member of a three-judge בית דין is not suspected of bias, as the משנה in יבמות shows about a judge marrying a woman. So the owner on a panel of three should be allowed to inspect his own בכור.

steps.title: The ברייתא is about a single expert
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא means one person who is an expert (יחיד מומחה), who may permit others' בכורות but not his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, it means one person. As רב חסדא said in the name of רבי יוחנן, it can be done by one expert. Here too, it means one expert.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Steps 11–13. The ברייתא is about one person who is a recognized expert.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 asked: one ordinary person is not trusted on any בכור, so why say 'except his own'? Step 13 asked: a panel of three is not suspected, so why exclude his own? The answer is a third case. One expert may rule alone, so his decision is fully his own, and that is why he is suspected when the animal is his.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually. Introduces an answer that keeps the first idea.
With one person
A single recognized expert who may rule alone
Here too

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up 'one ordinary person' (Step 12) with 'one expert' (here). The ordinary person is not trusted on anyone's בכור. The expert is trusted on everyone's בכור except his own.
steps.whyThisMatters: This defines who the ברייתא is talking about. Everything after this explains the rest of the ברייתא about this same expert.

phrases.english: Really, it is speaking of one person,

phrases.aramaic: וְכִדְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: as Rav Chisda said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
phrases.notes: That statement was about releasing vows (התרת נדרים).

phrases.english: it can be done by a single expert,
here too, it means a single expert.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem from Steps 12–13 by naming a third case: one expert.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case (one expert, not one ordinary person and not three judges)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case had to be either one ordinary person or a panel of three, and both options caused problems.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is one expert. He may permit others' בכורות alone, so he is suspected only for his own.

steps.title: Why he may inspect his own קדשים
steps.stepSummary: He may inspect his own קדשים because he could have the הקדש annulled anyway, so he has no reason to lie.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he may inspect his own holy animals. This is because, if he wanted, he could ask a חכם to annul his הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the next line of the ברייתא. It says why the owner is trusted on his own קדשים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think he would falsely find a blemish so the animal leaves קדושה. But he does not need to lie: he can go to a חכם and have his הקדש annulled (שאלה). With an easy honest way out, there is no reason to suspect him.

keyTerms.meaning: His own holy (dedicated) animals
If he wanted
He can ask a חכם to annul his dedication of them

phrases.english: And he may inspect his own holy animals,
because if he wanted, he could ask to have their dedication annulled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to explain the next clause of the ברייתא from Step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Removes the suspicion by showing he has no real motive
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He might lie about a blemish to get his animal out of קדושה.
steps.terutzMaskana: He could annul the הקדש honestly, so he gains nothing by lying.

steps.title: Why he may inspect his own מעשר
steps.stepSummary: He may inspect his own מעשר animals because he could have blemished his whole herd beforehand.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he may inspect his own מעשר animals. This is because, if he wanted, he could put a blemish on his whole flock.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the next line of the ברייתא. It says why the owner is trusted on his own מעשר בהמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before he separates מעשר, the animals are still ordinary. He may legally blemish all of them, and then the מעשר animal would not go on the מזבח. Since he could avoid bringing a קרבן this way, he has no reason to lie about a blemish.

keyTerms.meaning: His own animal tithes (מעשר בהמה)
He could put a blemish on it
His flock / herd

phrases.english: And his own tithe animals,
because if he wanted, he could put a blemish
on his entire flock.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same pattern as Step 15, now for מעשר.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Removes the suspicion by showing he has no real motive
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He might lie about a blemish to keep his מעשר animal from being a קרבן.
steps.terutzMaskana: He could have blemished the whole herd before tithing, so lying gains him nothing.

steps.title: Why he may rule on his own טהרות
steps.stepSummary: He may decide on the purity of his own food because he could still eat it when he himself is impure.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he may be asked about his own pure foods. This is because the food is still fit for him during his days of טומאה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the last line of the ברייתא. It says why the owner is trusted to rule on his own טהרות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if his food became טמא, it is not lost. He can still eat it when he himself is טמא. Since he loses little either way, he has no strong reason to falsely call it טהור.

keyTerms.meaning: He may be asked / may rule
His own foods kept in purity
They are fit for him
The days when he himself is impure

steps.whatToRemember: One expert (יחיד מומחה) may not permit his own בכור, because he has a real motive to lie. He is trusted on his own קדשים, מעשר, and טהרות, because in each case he has an honest way out or loses little, so there is no real motive to lie.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the principle behind the whole ברייתא. We suspect a person only where he has a real benefit from lying.

phrases.english: And he may be asked about his own pure foods,
because they are fit for him in his days of impurity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes explaining the clauses of the ברייתא, following Steps 15–16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Removes the suspicion by showing he has no real motive
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He might falsely call his food טהור to avoid losing it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The food stays usable for him while he is טמא, so the motive is too weak to suspect him.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the chapter עד כמה ישראל חייבין
steps.stepSummary: The formal closing line of the chapter עד כמה ישראל חייבין.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter 'עד כמה ישראל חייבין.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing the chapter about how long an owner must care for a בכור and related laws. This line is a closing formula, not an argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The discussion of an expert judging his own בכור, קדשים, מעשר and טהרות (steps 10-17) was the last topic of this chapter. 'הדרן עלך' marks that the chapter is over. A brand-new משנה starts right after it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We will return to you' — the formula said when finishing a chapter
'Until when is a Jew obligated' — the name of the chapter being closed

phrases.english: We will return to you,
[chapter] 'Until when is a Jew obligated.'

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ עַד כַּמָּה יִשְׂרָאֵל חַיָּיבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the chapter whose final sugya ended with step 17.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The chapter עד כמה ישראל חייבין is complete. A new chapter begins.

steps.title: Blemished sacred animals are sold and weighed like ordinary meat
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that all פסולי המוקדשין are sold, slaughtered and weighed in the public meat market, because the profit belongs to הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: All disqualified sacred animals — their profit goes to הקדש. They are sold in the meat market, slaughtered in the meat market, and weighed by the litra.
steps.whatsHappening: A new chapter opens with a new משנה. It says that redeemed blemished sacred animals may be sold in the busy butcher market and sold by weight, just like regular meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally we would not treat a once-holy animal like ordinary meat. But here the money from the sale goes to הקדש. So we let it be sold in the way that brings the highest price, so that הקדש does not lose money.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין — 'our משנה'; marks the start of the משנה text
Sacred animals that got a blemish, became unfit for the מזבח, and were redeemed
The profit from them goes to the Temple treasury
The butchers' market, where meat is sold publicly
A litra — a unit of weight; selling by exact weight like ordinary meat

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the animal is still fully holy here. It has a blemish and was redeemed, so it may be eaten. The משנה is only discussing how it may be sold.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main principle of the chapter: how the sale is handled depends on who receives the profit.

phrases.english: MISHNA: All disqualified consecrated animals —
their profit goes to the Temple treasury;
they are sold in the butchers' market and slaughtered in the butchers' market,
and are weighed by the litra,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new chapter and a new topic after the הדרן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: פסולי המוקדשין, whose profit goes to הקדש, may be sold and slaughtered in the market and sold by weight.

steps.title: Exception for firstborn and tithe animals, whose profit goes to the owner
steps.stepSummary: בכור and מעשר are excluded from market selling and weighing, because their profit goes to the owner. The משנה then repeats the contrast: פסולי המוקדשין profit goes to הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: Except for the בכור and the מעשר, whose profit goes to the owners. Disqualified sacred animals — their profit goes to הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives an exception to the rule it just stated. A blemished בכור or מעשר animal may not be sold in the market or by weight.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason is the profit. For בכור and מעשר the money goes to the private owner (the כהן, or the owner of the מעשר), so there is no Temple loss to protect against. We therefore do not allow treating holy meat like ordinary meat just to help a private person get a better price.

keyTerms.meaning: Except for
A firstborn male animal, given to a כהן
מעשר בהמה — the tithe of animals, which stays with the owner
Their profit goes to the owners

steps.whatToRemember: The key question is who gets the money. If it goes to הקדש, we allow market selling to protect הקדש. If it goes to the owner (בכור, מעשר), we do not.
steps.confusionAlert: The בכור and מעשר are still blemished sacred animals. They are an exception only in how they may be sold, not a different category of קדשים.

phrases.english: except for the firstborn and the animal tithe,
whose profit goes to the owners.
Disqualified consecrated animals — their profit goes to the Temple treasury.

steps.triggerLanguage: חוּץ מִן הַבְּכוֹר וְהַמַּעֲשֵׂר, שֶׁהֲנָיָיתָן לַבְּעָלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the rule of step 19 by excluding בכור and מעשר, and gives the reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Blemished בכור and מעשר are not sold in the market or by weight, because the profit goes to the owner and not to הקדש.

steps.title: Weighing one portion against another portion of firstborn meat
steps.stepSummary: Even though בכור meat may not be sold by weight, one may weigh one portion against another portion.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one may weigh a portion against a portion with the בכור.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a small allowance about בכור meat. Regular weighing by litra is forbidden, but balancing one piece against another piece is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What is forbidden is selling בכור meat the way ordinary butchers do, using standard weights. Putting one portion on the scale against another portion (for example, ordinary meat against בכור meat) is not how meat is normally sold. So it does not count as treating the בכור like ordinary meat.

keyTerms.meaning: One weighs
A portion against a portion — balancing two pieces of meat on a scale

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the ban on weighing בכור meat is about not treating it like ordinary market meat, not a ban on using a scale at all.

phrases.english: And one may weigh a portion against a portion with the firstborn.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limited permission within the restriction on בכור given in step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Weighing a portion against a portion is permitted for בכור meat, even though selling it by standard weight is not.
